scenario_stem:
Amberley Farm Shop is a private limited company opened 3 years ago by Jenny Marland in Country X, selling home-grown vegetables, eggs and preserves to about 210 customers each week and employs 6 staff. It has current assets of $48,000 and current liabilities of $31,500. In June it expects cash inflows of $9,400 and cash outflows of $11,200, a net cash flow of -$1,800.

July begins with an opening balance of $2,600, with inflows forecast at $12,750 against outflows of $8,900. Jenny plans a $26,000 cold-room purchase due in August but worries the shop cannot cover it. She is considering an overdraft from her bank or asking 60 debtors who owe money to pay sooner, and postponing the cold room by six months is the third option.

questions.question_text: Define 'net cash flow'.
questions.model_answer: Net cash flow is the difference between a business's total cash inflows and its total cash outflows over a period of time (for Amberley Farm Shop, $12,750 inflows minus $8,900 outflows gives a net cash flow of +$3,850 in July). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Net cash flow is total inflows minus total outflows over a period
A positive net cash flow means more cash came in than went out during the period

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Amberley Farm Shop could overcome its short-term cash shortfall in June.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Amberley Farm Shop could arrange an overdraft with its bank [k]; the June forecast shows outflows of $11,200 against inflows of only $9,400, so a facility of roughly $2,000 would cover the gap until July, when inflows of $12,750 are forecast to exceed outflows of $8,900 [app]. Way 2: the shop could ask its 60 debtors to settle sooner [k]; pulling those payments forward would lift June inflows above $11,200, removing the -$1,800 deficit without borrowing [app].

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft lets a business spend more than its bank balance up to an agreed limit
Asking debtors to pay faster speeds up cash inflows
application_max_2: Applies the June figures: $11,200 outflows vs $9,400 inflows, roughly a $2,000 gap
Applies the 60 debtors and the -$1,800 June net cash flow to the faster-payment option

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Amberley Farm Shop of preparing a cash-flow forecast.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: a forecast shows the shortfall before it happens [k]; because the June deficit of $1,800 would be visible in advance, Jenny can arrange an overdraft or chase the 60 debtors before wages and supplier bills fall due [app][an]. Benefit 2: it helps decide whether the $26,000 cold-room purchase in August is affordable [k]; the July closing balance will be about $6,450 (opening $2,600 plus net cash flow of +$3,850), far below the purchase price, so the forecast tells her extra finance or a postponement is essential [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A cash-flow forecast highlights periods of expected shortage or surplus in advance
It supports decisions about large or irregular purchases
application_max_2: Applies the June deficit of $1,800 and the 60 debtors as early-warning use
Applies the July closing balance of about $6,450 against the $26,000 cold-room price
analysis_max_2: Explains that early warning allows action before the shortfall hits
Explains that a $26,000 purchase cannot be met from a $6,450 closing balance without new finance

questions.question_text: Do you think Jenny should buy the cold room now using an overdraft, or postpone it by six months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Jenny could argue the cold room should be bought now so it is ready for the August vegetable peak [k]. However, the forecast shows only $2,600 opening in July and a +$3,850 net cash flow, so a $26,000 payment would swallow all available cash and push the shop deeper into overdraft while June is already forecast at -$1,800 [app][an]. Postponing six months protects the thin position and lets the shop build its balance from the stronger July forecast of $12,750 inflows, though it delays the extra capacity a growing shop with 210 customers may need [app][an]. Because postponement is reversible and cheap, whereas an overdraft is not guaranteed [k][eval], the sensible decision is to postpone the cold room until autumn sales are banked and only then confirm the purchase [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying now secures the equipment before the August peak
Postponement is a reversible, low-cost way to manage cash shortage
application_max_2: Applies the $2,600 July opening balance and +$3,850 net cash flow against the $26,000 price
Applies the June -$1,800 deficit and the $12,750 July inflows to the postponement option
analysis_max_2: Explains that a $26,000 payment cannot be funded from a $6,450 July closing balance
Explains that postponement lets cash rebuild from July inflows before committing
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to the reversibility of postponing and the risk of overdraft reliance
Recognises the trade-off with the August capacity need

scenario_stem:
Bluewater Surf School is a sole trader business run by Kai Delgado on the coast of Country X, teaching surf lessons to about 480 pupils each April-to-September season. Kai employs 4 instructors. His forecast shows July inflows of $18,600 against outflows of $13,400, August inflows of $15,200 against outflows of $14,750, and September inflows of only $6,800 against outflows of $9,900. He begins September with an opening balance of $7,900.

The school has current assets of $22,000 and current liabilities of $14,500, leaving working capital of $7,500. Kai wants to buy two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each in October, but the quiet winter months worry him. He is considering delaying the purchase until the spring term or taking out a small bank overdraft to cover the off-season shortfall.

questions.question_text: Define 'opening balance'.
questions.model_answer: Opening balance is the cash a business has available at the start of a period, brought forward from the previous period's closing balance (Bluewater Surf School begins September with $7,900). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Opening balance is the cash held at the start of a period
The opening balance equals the previous closing balance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why September is the hardest month of the season for Bluewater Surf School's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: demand collapses once the season ends [k]; the forecast shows September inflows of only $6,800 against $18,600 in July and $15,200 in August [app]. Reason 2: outflows are slower to fall than inflows [k]; September outflows of $9,900 still exceed inflows, giving a net cash flow of -$3,100 and leaving a September closing balance of only $4,800 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Seasonal businesses see demand fall sharply when the season ends
Fixed-style outflows (wages, storage) continue when revenue falls
application_max_2: Applies the fall in inflows from $18,600 (July) and $15,200 (August) to $6,800 (September)
Applies September outflows of $9,900 vs inflows of $6,800, i.e. -$3,100 and closing $4,800

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Kai could overcome the cash-flow problem he expects in September.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Kai could ask his bank for an overdraft [k]; this covers the September shortfall of $3,100 so the school keeps paying instructors and boat maintenance while it waits for next season's deposits [app][an]. Way 2: he could delay buying the two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each until spring [k]; postponing this $6,800 capital item protects the $7,500 working capital and keeps September liquid [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft or bank loan provides short-term finance for a cash-flow gap
Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflow
application_max_2: Applies the $3,100 September shortfall ($9,900 outflows vs $6,800 inflows)
Applies the $3,400 boards x 2 = $6,800 against the $7,500 working capital
analysis_max_2: Explains that an overdraft bridges the gap until next season's income arrives
Explains that delaying a discretionary purchase is a cheaper way to protect cash

questions.question_text: Do you think Kai should buy the two rescue boards in October, or delay until the spring term? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Kai could argue the boards should be bought now, before the winter, because they are essential safety equipment for a school teaching 480 pupils and because October prices may rise [k]. The forecast offers little room: September closes at $4,800, already below the $6,800 cost of the boards, so both would be paid for out of a $7,500 working capital, cutting it to under $1,000 [app][an]. However, delaying to spring protects the cash position through the worst months, risks only a seven-month delay to the purchase and still lands in time for next season [app][an]. Because the boards are important but not needed until lessons restart [k], the evidence favours delaying to the spring term unless the bank confirms an overdraft in writing [eval]; overcommitting in the off-season would jeopardise instructor wages [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Rescue boards are safety-critical equipment that cannot be postponed indefinitely
Delaying capital expenditure is a standard remedy for a short-term cash shortage
application_max_2: Applies the September closing balance of $4,800 vs the $6,800 board cost
Applies working capital of $7,500 falling to under $1,000 if both boards are bought
analysis_max_2: Explains that buying now would require (or dangerously assume) overdraft funding
Explains that delay costs reputation little but protects instructor wages and bills
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to the off-season cash constraint and the seasonal cycle
Weighs equipment safety against solvency and the overdraft condition

scenario_stem:
Redbank Construction Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by Marta Okoro in Country X, employing 38 staff across two housing sites and a small joinery workshop. The business has current assets of $96,000 including $34,000 owed by debtors, against current liabilities of $58,000. Its largest client, a housing association, settles invoices 60 days late. March inflows are forecast at $21,500 against outflows of $29,300.

Redbank begins April with an opening balance of $5,100 and forecasts April inflows of $27,800 against outflows of $22,400. Marta is considering offering the housing association a 2% early-payment discount to bring the $34,000 in sooner, taking a $20,000 bank loan, or delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order until the association pays. She must decide before the April payroll.

questions.question_text: Define 'closing balance'.
questions.model_answer: Closing balance is the cash a business has at the end of a period, found by adding the net cash flow to the opening balance (Redbank begins April with $5,100 and April's forecast net cash flow is +$5,400, giving a closing balance of $10,500). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Closing balance is the cash remaining at the end of a period
Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redbank Construction of offering the 2% early-payment discount to the housing association.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: the discount should pull cash in sooner [k]; the housing association is 60 days late and owes $34,000, so pulling even half into April would more than cover the $22,400 of April outflows [app]. Benefit 2: a 2% discount is cheap finance [k]; giving up $680 on $34,000 costs far less than the interest on a $20,000 bank loan and still lands before the April payroll [app].

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount encourages debtors to pay faster, improving cash flow
A small discount can be cheaper than interest on borrowed finance
application_max_2: Applies the $34,000 owed and 60 days late payment by the housing association
Applies 2% of $34,000 = $680 against the $22,400 April outflows and $20,000 loan

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order could help Redbank's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: delaying postpones a very large capital outflow [k]; moving the $32,000 mixer out of April keeps April outflows at $22,400 and lets the forecast opening balance of $5,100 recover to about $10,500 without new borrowing [app][an]. Reason 2: it avoids committing before the association pays [k]; with the client 60 days late on $34,000, delaying the purchase means Redbank is not forced into a $20,000 loan before knowing when cash will actually arrive [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure is a remedy for a short-term cash-flow problem
Avoiding new long-term borrowing reduces interest costs and insolvency risk
application_max_2: Applies the $32,000 mixer vs April outflows of $22,400 and opening balance of $5,100
Applies the association's 60-day lateness and the $34,000 owed to the loan alternative
analysis_max_2: Explains that delaying pushes the large outflow beyond the strained month
Explains that commitment before payment risks inability to fund the April payroll

questions.question_text: Do you think Marta should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $20,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marta could argue for the 2% early-payment discount because it tackles the root problem [k]. Costing only $680 on $34,000, it is cheaper than a $20,000 loan, avoids new debt and matches the fact that the housing association is already 60 days late [app][an]. However, the discount only helps if the association agrees and pays promptly, so if it still pays slowly the April payroll remains at risk and a loan - or the mixer delay - may still be needed [app][an]. Because the discount is cheap and non-binding while the mixer delay alone does not guarantee cash [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the discount first and taking the $20,000 loan only if the association refuses [eval]; the decision should be made before the April payroll, not after it.

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount is a cheap way to speed up debtors without new debt
A bank loan gives certain finance but adds interest and repayment obligations
application_max_2: Applies 2% of $34,000 = $680 vs interest on a $20,000 loan
Applies the payroll deadline and the association's 60-day lateness
analysis_max_2: Explains that the discount is cheap only if the association accepts and pays early
Explains that the loan guarantees funding but at extra cost and does nothing to fix late payment
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation sequencing discount first, loan as fallback
Weighs certainty of the loan against the cheapness and uncertainty of the discount

scenario_stem:
Saffron Spice Restaurant is an independent curry house in Country X opened 6 years ago by brothers Dev and Priya Nair, serving about 95 covers on a busy Saturday and 40 covers on weekdays, with both brothers working the stoves six nights a week. It rents rather than owns its kitchen equipment and turns over $38,000 a month. Current assets are $15,600 and current liabilities are $19,200.

After a roof leak in February, the Nairs face an unexpected $7,400 repair bill. The February forecast shows inflows of $31,800 against outflows of $34,600, while March forecasts $36,500 inflows against $33,100 outflows. They are deciding between a $9,000 bank overdraft and asking the spice wholesaler for a further 45 days credit before paying their February bill.

questions.question_text: Define 'overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft is a short-term bank facility allowing a business to withdraw more money than it holds in its account, up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount borrowed. [2]

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft is a short-term bank facility to spend more than the balance
Interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by the restaurant's negative working capital position.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: current liabilities exceed current assets [k]; the restaurant holds only $15,600 of current assets against $19,200 of short-term debts, so working capital is negative at -$3,600 [app]. Problem 2: the business runs a cash deficit before the repair bill is paid [k]; February outflows of $34,600 already exceed inflows of $31,800, so the February net cash flow of -$2,800 plus the $7,400 roof bill means new finance is needed [app].

knowledge_max_2: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities; negative means short-term debts exceed short-term assets
Negative working capital risks inability to pay debts as they fall due
application_max_2: Applies $15,600 vs $19,200 giving working capital of -$3,600
Applies February inflows of $31,800 and outflows of $34,600 (-$2,800) plus the $7,400 repair

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the $9,000 overdraft compared with asking the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: the overdraft lets the repair proceed immediately without starving the kitchen [k]; the February gap of -$2,800 and the $7,400 bill mean a $9,000 facility covers both [app][an]. Benefit 2: it keeps the supplier relationship intact [k]; asking the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit risks delayed or refused spice deliveries exactly when the March forecast of $36,500 inflows depends on full service, while March outflows of $33,100 still fall due [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft is flexible short-term finance matched to the cash gap
Delaying supplier payments can damage the supplier relationship and supply of goods
application_max_2: Applies the -$2,800 February gap and the $7,400 repair vs the $9,000 overdraft
Applies March inflows of $36,500 and outflows of $33,100 to the delivery risk
analysis_max_2: Explains the overdraft covers both the deficit and the repair bill without affecting suppliers
Explains refused credit could disrupt supply in the strongest trading month

questions.question_text: Do you think the Nairs should take the $9,000 overdraft, or ask the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Nairs could argue for the overdraft because it keeps the wholesaler relationship safe while fixing the roof immediately [k]. A $9,000 facility would cover the -$2,800 February deficit and the $7,400 repair, and interest is paid only on what is drawn [app][an]. However, an overdraft is repayable on demand and adds a fixed monthly cost, so if March disappoints below the $36,500 inflow forecast the bank could call the facility in [app][an]. Because the wholesaler credit would cost nothing if granted but risks refusal and reputational damage [k][eval], the evidence favours taking the $9,000 overdraft now, agreed in writing, while honouring the March payment to the wholesaler in full [eval]; the decision should be reversed only if the bank refuses or prices the facility punitively.

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft provides immediate short-term finance but is repayable on demand
Asking suppliers for more credit is free but damages the business relationship
application_max_2: Applies the $9,000 overdraft to the -$2,800 February deficit and $7,400 repair
Applies the March forecast of $36,500 inflows / $33,100 outflows to the overdraft risk
analysis_max_2: Explains the overdraft covers both the deficit and the repair without touching the supplier
Explains that a call-in risk exists if March underperforms
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to writing, cost comparison and relationship risk
Weighs overdraft certainty against supplier-credit cost and risk of refusal

scenario_stem:
Larkspur Florist is a partnership owned by Emma and Lucy Hartley in Country X, selling fresh flowers, wedding arrangements and weekly office subscriptions. It forecasts May inflows of $8,700 including $1,900 from two weddings against outflows of $10,300, and June inflows of $9,800 against outflows of $8,150; it also sells wedding corsages all year round. It begins May with an opening balance of $2,000 and employs 2 full-time florists.

The partnership has current assets of $12,400 and current liabilities of $7,900. Emma wants a refrigerated display cabinet costing $4,500 to cut flower wastage, but buying it now would use most of the remaining cash. The Hartleys are considering postponing the cabinet for three months, or switching office subscribers to weekly rather than monthly payment.

questions.question_text: Calculate the forecast closing balance for May. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Closing balance for May = opening balance + net cash flow = $2,000 + ($8,700 - $10,300) = $2,000 - $1,600 = $400. [2]

knowledge_max_2: May net cash flow = $8,700 inflows - $10,300 outflows = -$1,600
Closing balance = $2,000 opening + (-$1,600) = $400

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the May closing balance is forecast to be so low.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: May outflows exceed inflows [k]; the forecast shows $10,300 of outflows against $8,700 of inflows, a net cash flow of -$1,600 [app]. Reason 2: wedding takings are uneven and do not cover the month [k]; although May includes $1,900 from two weddings, office subscriptions are billed monthly, so cash received cannot absorb the flower, wage and delivery costs before the month closes [app].

knowledge_max_2: A cash-flow deficit month makes the closing balance low
Mismatch in timing between when money is owed and received lowers the closing balance
application_max_2: Applies $10,300 outflows vs $8,700 inflows = -$1,600 net cash flow
Applies the $1,900 wedding income and monthly-billed subscriptions to the timing gap

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the Hartleys could improve the florist's cash flow in June.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: switching office subscribers to weekly rather than monthly payment pulls cash in sooner [k]; collecting subscriptions weekly instead of monthly smooths inflows and could lift May's and June's balances well above $400 and $2,050 respectively [app][an]. Way 2: postponing the refrigerated cabinet purchase cuts outflows [k]; holding the $4,500 cabinet spend out of May, a deficit month, keeps cash in the partnership until June's forecast net cash flow of +$1,650 arrives [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing the time taken to collect receivables speeds up cash inflows
Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflows
application_max_2: Applies weekly vs monthly subscriptions to inflow timing and closing balance
Applies the $4,500 cabinet against May's -$1,600 net cash flow and June's +$1,650
analysis_max_2: Explains weekly billing accelerates cash without discounting
Explains delaying the cabinet avoids spending in the weakest month

questions.question_text: Do you think Emma and Lucy should buy the refrigerated display cabinet now, or postpone it for three months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Hartleys could argue for buying the cabinet now because it cuts wastage in a flower business where stock perishes quickly [k]. But the May forecast closing balance is only $400 after a -$1,600 net cash flow, so the $4,500 cabinet would consume more than the entire balance and leave nothing for weekly wages [app][an]. However, buying in June or July is feasible once June's +$1,650 net cash flow lifts the balance back above $2,000, and switching subscribers to weekly payment would help further [app][an]. Because the cabinet is an efficiency upgrade rather than a survival need [k][eval], the evidence favours postponing it for three months and revisiting the purchase once the weekly subscriptions are running [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying now reduces wastage but suits only businesses with spare cash
Postponement preserves cash during a deficit month
application_max_2: Applies the $400 May closing balance vs the $4,500 cabinet price
Applies June's +$1,650 and the switch to weekly subscriptions to the delay option
analysis_max_2: Explains the cabinet would drain the whole cash position immediately
Explains waiting restores affordability without abandoning the efficiency gain
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to postpone tied to the priority of wages over upgrades
Acknowledges the wastage benefit and the reassessment trigger

scenario_stem:
Northgate Veterinary Clinic is a private limited company opened 8 years ago by Dr Tom Whitfield in Country X, treating about 70 animals a week and vaccinating local farm herds. October inflows are forecast at $26,400 against outflows of $24,100, and November inflows at $24,900 against outflows of $27,600. The clinic begins October with an opening balance of $3,300 and is owed $9,800 by farm clients on 45-day terms.

The clinic has current assets of $34,500 against current liabilities of $17,000. Dr Whitfield wants to buy a digital X-ray machine for $28,000, which his supplier will sell on 60-day credit instead of for cash now. He is deciding whether to take the credit deal or wait a year and put the money towards a part-time nurse's wages instead.

questions.question_text: Define 'debtors'.
questions.model_answer: Debtors are customers or clients who owe a business money because they have received goods or services on credit but have not yet paid (Northgate Veterinary Clinic is owed $9,800 by farm clients on 45-day terms). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Debtors owe money to a business for goods or services already supplied
Debtors appear as a current asset until payment is received

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the clinic of asking farm clients to pay the $9,800 they owe more quickly.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: asking debtors to pay faster brings cash forward [k]; Northgate is owed $9,800 on 45-day terms, and November needs it most because November inflows of $24,900 trail outflows of $27,600 [app]. Benefit 2: it reduces the need to borrow [k]; collecting even part of the $9,800 would more than cover the -$2,700 November net cash flow and protect the $3,300 opening balance [app].

knowledge_max_2: Asking debtors to pay faster speeds up cash inflows
Faster collection reduces reliance on borrowing or overdrafts
application_max_2: Applies the $9,800 owed on 45-day terms to November's gap ($24,900 vs $27,600)
Applies -$2,700 November net cash flow and the $3,300 October opening balance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Dr Whitfield might wait a year before buying the X-ray machine.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the machine is unaffordable from current cash [k]; at $28,000 it is far beyond the October closing balance of about $5,600, so buying cash now would exhaust the $17,500 working capital [app][an]. Reason 2: waiting a year has a real opportunity cost he can weigh [k]; the $28,000 could fund a part-time nurse's wages in the meantime, lifting service quality while a smaller credit deal is negotiated again next year [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A large purchase may exceed available cash and working capital
Deferring a purchase frees resources for other priorities (opportunity cost)
application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 price vs October closing balance of about $5,600 and $17,500 working capital
Applies the $28,000 vs part-time nurse's wages alternative
analysis_max_2: Explains the purchase would leave the clinic dangerously under-funded
Explains the nurse alternative delivers value sooner and keeps options open

questions.question_text: Do you think Dr Whitfield should buy the X-ray machine now on 60-day credit, or wait a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Dr Whitfield could argue for the 60-day credit now because the machine improves diagnoses and could attract more farm clients [k]. The credit deal avoids an immediate $28,000 outflow, but the full price falls due 60 days later, when the November forecast shows a -$2,700 net cash flow and the $9,800 farm debt may not yet have landed [app][an]. However, borrowing $28,000 for one item against a $17,500 working capital leaves the clinic exposed if a farm client pays late, and delaying a year lets cash build from the October surplus of +$2,300 [app][an]. Because the farm vaccination income is seasonal and the machine is a discretionary purchase [k][eval], the evidence favours taking the credit deal only after confirming the $9,800 is collected early; otherwise waiting is safer [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Trade credit spreads a large purchase over time
A discretionary purchase can be deferred without breaking the business
application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 60-day credit falling due around November's -$2,700 net cash flow
Applies the $17,500 working capital and the $9,800 farm debt collection timing
analysis_max_2: Explains the machine benefit must be weighed against the crunch at payment date
Explains that collecting debtors first de-risks the credit deal
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditioned on collecting the $9,800 first
Weighs strategic benefit against seasonal cash risk and limited working capital

scenario_stem:
Willowbrook Children's Nursery is a social enterprise in Country X founded 5 years ago by Hannah Bhatt, providing affordable childcare for 64 children on a low-income estate. Parent fees cover most monthly costs and a community trust funds the shortfall. Current assets are $27,300 against current liabilities of $13,800. January inflows are forecast at $14,200 against outflows of $16,900, and February forecasts inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $16,200.

The nursery begins January with an opening balance of $4,700. Hannah wants to replace ageing outdoor play equipment for $9,000, but January's deficit leaves little spare cash. A local trust has offered a grant of $4,500 if she applies before 31 March; alternatively the bank will lend $5,000 repayable over 12 months at 8% interest.

questions.question_text: Define 'current assets'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets are resources owned by a business that are expected to be converted into cash within one year, such as stock, debtors and money in the bank (Willowbrook Children's Nursery has $27,300 in current assets). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current assets are expected to be turned into cash within one year
Examples include cash, debtors and stock

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Willowbrook's cash flow is weaker in January than in February.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: fees fall after the holiday period [k]; January inflows of $14,200 are well below February's $18,500, so children's fees simply do not cover the bills in a quiet month [app]. Reason 2: winter outflows are higher [k]; January outflows of $16,900 exceed both its inflows and February's outflows of $16,200, so the January deficit of $2,700 is driven by the gap between falling inflows and stubborn costs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Seasonal dips in income can create a deficit month
High fixed or winter costs keep outflows elevated when income falls
application_max_2: Applies January inflows of $14,200 vs February's $18,500
Applies January outflows of $16,900 vs February's $16,200 and the $2,700 deficit

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the grant compared with the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: the grant is not repayable [k]; unlike the $5,000 loan, the grant of $4,500 adds cash without creating a new outflow, protecting the end-of-January balance of $2,000 [app][an]. Benefit 2: it avoids interest and fixed repayments [k]; dodging the 8% interest on $5,000 ($400 a year) and twelve monthly repayments in a February deficit month keeps the nursery's tight working capital of $13,500 intact [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A grant does not have to be repaid
A loan creates repayments and interest that worsen cash flow
application_max_2: Applies the $4,500 grant vs loan of $5,000 and the $2,000 January closing balance
Applies 8% interest on $5,000 = $400 and twelve repayments against $13,500 working capital
analysis_max_2: Explains the grant protects cash without new obligations
Explains loan repayments would worsen an already deficit month

questions.question_text: Do you think Hannah should apply for the grant, or take the $5,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hannah could argue for the grant because it is effectively free money and suits a social enterprise [k]. Applying before 31 March secures $4,500 with no interest and no repayments, which suits a nursery whose January deficit is forecast at $2,700 and whose January closing balance will be only $2,000 [app][an]. However, the grant is not guaranteed, takes time to process and may arrive after the equipment decision must be made, while the loan at 8% interest is certain and funds the $9,000 purchase immediately [app][an]. Because the equipment is not urgently required and the January deficit must be managed first [k][eval], the evidence favours applying for the grant while keeping the loan as a written fallback if the application fails [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grants are non-repayable finance well suited to social enterprises
A loan is certain but adds interest and repayment pressure
application_max_2: Applies the $4,500 grant, 31 March deadline and the $2,700 January deficit
Applies the $2,000 January closing balance and the $9,000 equipment cost
analysis_max_2: Explains the grant preserves cash but is slow and uncertain
Explains the loan is fast but increases the fixed outflow burden
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to apply for the grant with the loan as fallback
Weighs certainty vs cost in the context of the January deficit

scenario_stem:
Eastcliffe Boatyard Ltd is an 11-year-old business in Country X, on an estuary at the mouth of the River Alder, run by managing director Rosa Jimenez. It repairs 30 yachts a year and stores 18 boats ashore each winter. Current assets are $61,000 including $19,000 owed by boat owners, and current liabilities are $44,000. December inflows are forecast at $7,600 against outflows of $13,900, and January at $5,400 against $9,700.

The yard begins December with an opening balance of $12,500. Rosa is considering a 20% winter service discount to fill idle slipways, and she plans a February bulk buy of $8,500 in paint and antifoul. She could instead delay the bulk buy to April, or press boat owners to settle the $19,000 they owe before offering any discount.

questions.question_text: Outline two ways the boatyard could overcome its winter cash shortfall.
questions.model_answer: The boatyard could offer a winter service discount to pull in cash from yacht owners who pay now rather than after the work, and it could delay the February bulk buy of paint and antifoul to April so the $8,500 stays in the business during the weakest months. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Offering discounts or faster debtor collection raises short-term cash inflows
Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflows

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the boatyard of pressing boat owners to settle the $19,000 they owe before offering the discount.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: pressing debtors converts sales into cash [k]; $19,000 is owed by boat owners, and collecting it would more than cover January's forecast shortfall of -$4,300 [app]. Benefit 2: it strengthens February without giving away margin [k]; if the $19,000 arrives, the planned $8,500 February bulk buy could be funded from banked cash rather than an overdraft, instead of pairing a 20% discount with an already weak January closing balance of only $1,900 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Pressing debtors to pay faster is a core remedy for a short-term cash shortage
Collecting debts before discounting protects profit margins
application_max_2: Applies the $19,000 owed vs January's -$4,300 net cash flow
Applies the $8,500 bulk buy vs the $1,900 January closing balance and the 20% discount

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the February bulk buy of $8,500 in paint and antifoul could cause.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: the cash is not there yet [k]; Eastcliffe closes January at only $1,900, so an $8,500 February bulk buy would create a gap of over $6,600 even if every owner paid on time, forcing an overdraft [app][an]. Problem 2: the money would be locked up in slow-moving stock [k]; tying $8,500 into paint and antifoul during the weakest trading months cuts the working capital of $17,000 and leaves less headroom for December and January wages [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Spending cash before it is earned creates an unfunded outflow
Bulk buying ties up working capital in stock that sells slowly
application_max_2: Applies the $8,500 bulk buy vs the $1,900 January closing balance
Applies working capital of $17,000 (from $61,000 current assets and $44,000 current liabilities)
analysis_max_2: Explains the bulk buy would be funded by borrowing, adding cost and risk
Explains stock ties up cash needed for wages in the winter months

questions.question_text: Do you think Rosa should buy the paint and antifoul in February, or wait until April? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Rosa could argue for the February bulk buy because paint and antifoul are cheaper in bulk and the yard must be ready for the spring rush [k]. However, the forecast shows December's net cash flow at -$6,300 and January's at -$4,300, closing January at only $1,900, so the $8,500 would sit entirely on an overdraft [app][an]. Delaying to April defers the purchase to when spring repairs generate revenue, and lets Rosa first chase owners for the $19,000 owed, rebuilding March liquidity [app][an]. Because the yard cannot fund the bulk buy from winter cash [k][eval], the evidence favours delaying the purchase to April and buying only what February work strictly needs, funded by July collections rather than new credit [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Bulk buying can lower unit costs but strains cash
Deferring a purchase is a recognised remedy for off-season cash shortage
application_max_2: Applies December (-$6,300) and January (-$4,300) net cash flow and the $1,900 January closing balance
Applies the $19,000 owed by boat owners to the April/March recovery option
analysis_max_2: Explains the February bulk buy must be funded by overdraft given the winter deficit
Explains waiting aligns the purchase with the spring revenue cycle
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to cash availability rather than bulk-buy discounts
Acknowledges the spring preparation benefit lost by delaying

scenario_stem:
Marigold Bakery & Patisserie is a private limited company founded 4 years ago in Country X by Samira Chaudhry, supplying 14 supermarkets with bread and celebration cakes. Its ovens run from 4 a.m. and supermarket invoices are paid 30 days late. Current assets are $52,000 and current liabilities are $29,000. March inflows are forecast at $41,200 against outflows of $46,700, and April at $48,900 against $43,300; the bakery begins March with an opening balance of $6,400.

Samira's two largest supermarket chains owe the bakery $23,500 between them. She is considering a 4% early-payment discount to bring the money in sooner, a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest, and postponing the $11,000 mixer replacement by six months. She must decide before the March payroll is due.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to convert its assets into cash quickly and to meet its short-term debts as they fall due (current liabilities of $29,000 must be payable out of current assets of $52,000). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Liquidity is how quickly assets can be turned into cash
Liquidity measures the ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the bakery of offering the 4% early-payment discount.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: cash arrives sooner [k]; instead of waiting 30 days late, the bakery collects part of the $23,500 owed before the March payroll, lifting the March closing balance above the forecast $900 [app]. Benefit 2: the discount is cheaper than the alternative finance [k]; a 4% discount costs $940, while a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest costs $2,250 a year, so the discount saves about $1,310 [app].

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount speeds up cash inflows from debtors
A small discount can cost less than interest on a loan
application_max_2: Applies $23,500 owed and the closing balance of only $900 vs the March payroll

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of the 4% early-payment discount for the bakery.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: the discount directly reduces profit [k]; giving up $940 of margin on $23,500 assumes both chains take the discount and pay on time, and the bakery still needs cash for the March payroll [app][an]. Drawback 2: it may set a precedent [k]; if the two largest supermarket chains expect a 4% discount every month, the $940 loss repeats while the April recovery of +$5,600 net cash flow is no guarantee that future invoices come in quickly [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount sacrifices profit to improve cash flow
Repeated discounts set a costly precedent with large customers
application_max_2: Applies $940 cost of the discount vs both chains taking it and the March payroll
Applies the repeat cost vs April's +$5,600 net cash flow forecast
analysis_max_2: Explains the saving is only real if chains accept and pay quickly
Explains repeated discounting compounds the margin loss

questions.question_text: Do you think Samira should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $25,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Samira could argue for the early-payment discount because it fixes the root cause - slow-paying supermarkets [k]. At 4% it costs $940, far below the $2,250 annual interest on the $25,000 loan, and every pound collected early improves the March closing balance forecast at only $900 [app][an]. However, the discount works only if the chains agree and pay promptly, so uptake may be weak and a loan could still be needed to bridge the $5,500 March deficit [app][an]. Because the discount is cheaper and strengthens the customer relationship [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the 4% discount now while arranging a standby overdraft in case uptake is slow, keeping the $25,000 loan, and the $11,000 mixer postponement, as back-up options [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Early discounting targets the cause of the shortfall rather than its symptoms
A standby facility is a cheaper form of contingency than an unconditional loan
application_max_2: Applies $940 cost vs $2,250 loan interest and the $900 March closing balance
Applies the $5,500 March deficit and the $11,000 mixer postponement as fallback
analysis_max_2: Explains the discount is cheaper only if chains actually take it
Explains keeping the loan as back-up covers the risk of weak uptake
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation sequencing discount first, backup finance second
Weighs certain saving vs uncertain uptake in the supermarket chain context

scenario_stem:
Thornfield Freight is a private limited company operating 9 HGVs in Country X, delivering to supermarkets and builders' merchants across two provinces. January inflows are forecast at $34,600 against outflows of $39,800, while February inflows are $44,300 against outflows of $38,200. The business was founded 7 years ago and begins January with an opening balance of $8,900, with current assets of $74,000 and current liabilities of $41,000.

Thornfield owes its diesel supplier $28,000, due in late February. Customers owe the freight firm $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue. Marcus Vale, the managing director, must decide whether to delay the diesel payment by 30 days, press customers to settle the overdue $19,000 first, and postpone the $16,000 tyre replacement to April.

questions.question_text: Calculate the working capital for Thornfield Freight. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $74,000 - $41,000 = $33,000. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities
Working capital of $33,000 shows Thornfield's short-term resources exceed short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons for the negative net cash flow forecast in January.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: January outflows exceed inflows [k]; the forecast shows $39,800 of outflows against $34,600 of inflows, a net cash flow of -$5,200 [app]. Reason 2: customers pay late and do not cover the gap [k]; customers owe $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue, so January inflows barely reflect work already done [app].

knowledge_max_2: A net cash flow deficit occurs when outflows exceed inflows
Slow-paying debtors delay inflows even after work is done
application_max_2: Applies $34,600 inflows and $39,800 outflows = -$5,200 net cash flow
Applies $41,000 owed with $19,000 overdue over 60 days to the weak January inflows

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Thornfield could face if it delays the $28,000 diesel payment by 30 days.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: the supplier could refuse further deliveries [k]; delaying the $28,000 diesel payment by 30 days risks a stoppage, and without fuel the HGVs cannot complete the deliveries that generate February's $44,300 inflow [app][an]. Problem 2: postponement builds a larger bill [k]; the payment lands in February, when outflows already reach $38,200 against inflows of $44,300, so a late $28,000 payment on top could still strain the account despite the +$6,100 February net cash flow [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Delaying payments to suppliers risks refusal of future supplies
Postponing a payment does not remove the obligation, it just moves it
application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 diesel payment vs February's $44,300 inflow and the nine HGVs
Applies February outflows of $38,200 and the +$6,100 net cash flow to the extra $28,000
analysis_max_2: Explains a fuel cut-off would stop deliveries and revenue entirely
Explains February cannot absorb both its own bills and a deferred $28,000 comfortably

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should delay the diesel payment, or press customers to pay the overdue $19,000 first? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marcus could argue for delaying the diesel payment because suppliers often accept 30 days more credit and fleet operations matter most [k]. But the diesel supplier can stop deliveries immediately, halting the nine HGVs and putting the $34,600 January workload at risk, whereas the $19,000 owed to Thornfield is legally due already [app][an]. Chasing the overdue debts first brings in cash without interest or reputational risk, and even partial collection would cover the January net cash flow of -$5,200 [app][an]. Because the overdue customer debts are the cheaper and more certain source of cash [k][eval], the evidence favours pressing customers to settle the $19,000 while negotiating a written 30-day extension with the diesel supplier in parallel and keeping the $16,000 tyre replacement for April [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Delaying supplier payment is a common but risky remedy for a cash shortage
Collecting overdue debts is the safest way to raise cash without borrowing
application_max_2: Applies the nine HGVs and $34,600 January workload to the fuel cut-off risk
Applies the $19,000 overdue vs the -$5,200 January net cash flow
analysis_max_2: Explains unilateral non-payment risks the fleet halting entirely
Explains collecting the $19,000 closes the gap without new debt
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to chase debtors first with a parallel written supplier deal
Weighs supplier goodwill against debt collection certainty and cost
